title: I understand slopes. Why does everyone say a derivative is a rate of change?

question.body:
I can find the slope of a straight line using rise over run. But a curve has lots of different slopes, right?

I’m interested in how this connects to a car’s speedometer. What exactly is changing when we take a derivative?
question.priorKnowledge: Algebra, coordinates, and the slope of a straight line.

replies.body:
You already have the right starting point: **a curve has a slope at each point**, if it is differentiable there.

Imagine a graph of your car’s distance against time. The slope between two points is its *average* speed over that interval. Bring those points closer together, and you zoom in on the speed at one instant.

That limiting slope is the derivative. Your speedometer is giving you the everyday version of this idea.
But if the interval becomes zero, aren’t we dividing by zero? That is the bit that always loses me.

Great catch. We **never substitute a zero interval into the original fraction**. We ask what value the fraction approaches as the interval gets arbitrarily small.

For distance $s(t)=t^2$, the average speed from $t$ to $t+h$ is:

$$\frac{(t+h)^2-t^2}{h}=2t+h\quad(h\ne0)$$

As $h$ approaches zero, this approaches $2t$. So at $t=3$, the instantaneous speed is $6$ distance units per time unit.

The phrase **rate of change** also tells you the units. Distance divided by time gives speed; velocity divided by time gives acceleration.

A derivative always asks: *how much does the output change per small change in the input, near this point?*

Try this check: if the distance-time graph becomes flat for ten seconds, what should the speedometer read?
Zero! The distance is not changing even though time keeps moving. I think the graph connection finally makes sense.
